fix(executor): carry a failed attempt's reasons through an in-place restart

An in-place restart replaces the failure with a Queued phase so the TaskAction
stays non-terminal. The replacement was built from nothing, so the reasons the
failed attempt had accumulated went with it, and on this path they are the only
account of what happened that ever reaches the user: the failure itself is
discarded and never reported. For a GPU fault that means the line naming which
worker the hardware failed on was written and then thrown away, leaving a task
that appears to have restarted for no reason.

queuedForInPlaceRestart carries the reasons across and nothing else. The rest of
the failed attempt's task info stays behind on purpose, because its logs and custom
info describe the pod that has just been deleted rather than the one being queued.
Naming the conversion also gives it somewhere to be tested, which the path it is
inlined in does not have without an API server.

Skip Secret informer when ImagePullSecrets is disabled

The k8s client is only used by embedded_secret_manager's image-pull-secret
path, which is gated on EmbeddedSecretManagerConfig.ImagePullSecrets.Enabled.
When the feature is disabled the informer was generating list/watch traffic
for nothing, so only build the cache when the feature is on. In the disabled
path fall back to a bare direct client.

Also explicitly register the Secret informer with the cache. controller-
runtime caches are type-lazy (an informer is only started on first access),
so the previous code relied on the embedded secret manager being the only
caller. The explicit registration:
- documents that this cache is intended only for Secret reads
- ensures WaitForCacheSync actually blocks on the initial Secret list
  rather than returning immediately on an empty informer set, so the first
  admission isn't a guaranteed cache miss

feat(runs): capture full identity (name/email) in executed_by, not just subject

Decode the OIDC claims the load balancer forwards — sub, email, given_name,
family_name — and store the full common.EnrichedIdentity so RunDetails shows who
ran a task with their name and email, not just an opaque subject id. The standalone
runs service has no identity service to enrich a subject after the fact, so the
claims are captured at CreateRun from the token instead.

- identity.go: identityFromHeaders now decodes the signed x-amzn-oidc-data JWT
  (cookie path) or the forwarded Bearer token (SDK path) into User.Id.Subject +
  User.Spec{FirstName,LastName,Email}; still decoded, not re-verified. Falls back
  to x-amzn-oidc-identity (subject only) when the data header is absent.
- DB: new actions.executed_by BYTEA holding the serialized EnrichedIdentity;
  created_by keeps the bare subject for querying. CreateAction writes both.
- actionMetadataFromModel prefers the full executed_by, falling back to a
  subject-only identity for rows written before this column existed.

Names require the IdP to return given_name/family_name (e.g. ALB auth-scope must
include `profile`); email needs the `email` scope.

(one against the reference namespace, one against the pod namespace
for the mirrored copy). At admission scale this is unnecessary load
on the API server.

Replace the bare controller-runtime client.New with a cache-backed
delegating client. The cache is started for the lifetime of the
webhook and watches Secrets cluster-wide; reads are served from the
informer, writes still go through the API server.

fix(apps): run app pods under a configurable service account

The app deployment controller built the Knative pod spec without setting
serviceAccountName, so app pods ran under the namespace's `default` ServiceAccount.
On clusters using IRSA that SA has no role annotation, so the EKS webhook injects no
AWS_REGION or credentials — obstore then defaults to us-east-1 and the pod fails to
read its code bundle from object storage in another region (BareRedirect).

buildKService now sets ServiceAccountName from the app's own security context, or
the new internalApps.defaultServiceAccount config when the app doesn't request one.
This mirrors the executor's defaultK8sServiceAccount for task pods.

[BUG] array node eventing bump version (#5680)

* [BUG] add retries to handle array node eventing race condition (#421)

If there is an error updating a [FlyteWorkflow CRD](https://github.com/unionai/flyte/blob/6a7207c5345604a28a9d4e3699becff767f520f5/flytepropeller/pkg/controller/handler.go#L378), then the propeller streak ends without the CRD getting updated and the in-memory copy of the FlyteWorkflow is not utilized on the next loop.

[TaskPhaseVersion](https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte/blob/37b4e13ac4a3594ac63b7a35058f4b2220e51282/flytepropeller/pkg/apis/flyteworkflow/v1alpha1/node_status.go#L239) is stored in the FlyteWorkflow. This is incremented when there is an update to node/subnode state to ensure that events are unique. If the events stay in the same state and have the same TaskPhaseVersion, then they [get short-circuited and don't get emitted to admin](https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte/blob/37b4e13ac4a3594ac63b7a35058f4b2220e51282/flytepropeller/events/admin_eventsink.go#L59) or will get returned as an [AlreadyExists error](https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte/blob/37b4e13ac4a3594ac63b7a35058f4b2220e51282/flyteadmin/pkg/manager/impl/task_execution_manager.go#L172) and get [handled in propeller to not bubble up in an error](https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte/blob/37b4e13ac4a3594ac63b7a35058f4b2220e51282/flytepropeller/pkg/controller/nodes/node_exec_context.go#L38).

We can run into issues with ArrayNode eventing when:
- array node handler increments task phase version from "0" to "1"
- admin event sink emits event with version "1"
- the propeller controller is not able to update the FlyteWorkflow CRD, so the ArrayNodeStatus indicates taskPhaseVersion is still 0
- next loop, array node handler increments task phase version from "0" to "1"
- admin event sink prevents the event from getting emitted as an event with the same ID has already been received. No error is bubbled up.

This means we lose subnode state until there is an event that contains an update to that subnode. If the lost state is the subnode reaching a terminal state, then the subnode state (from admin/UI) is "stuck" in a non-terminal state.

I confirmed this to be an issue in the load-test-cluster. Whenever, there was an [error syncing the FlyteWorkflow](https://github.com/flyteorg/flyte/blob/37b4e13ac4a3594ac63b7a35058f4b2220e51282/flytepropeller/pkg/controller/workers.go#L91), the next round of eventing in ArrayNode would fail unless the ArrayNode phase changed.

Merge branch 'agent-sync-plugin' of https://github.com/Future-Outlier/flyte into agent-sync-plugin

Retry storage operation on transient idle connection error

Workflows with 100+ large (100MB+) file outputs lead to failures in the sidecar.
These failures appear to be due to transient errors during the upload phase.
Large file outputs (anything > 5MB) lead to a MultipartUpload, and flytecopilot
attempts to parallelize file uploads. However, it appears the parallelism causes
idle connections from a set of completed uploads to interfere with in-progress
connections for other uploads.

Since the failures are transient, implement a fix where copilot simply initiates
a retry (up to 5 max retries) if a transient error is seen during a flytecopilot
raw file upload. This fix is consistent with a similar issue seen previously in
Flyte storage writes: https://github.com/flyteorg/flyteadmin/pull/325

feat(copilot): add NAMED_DIR file input layout to preserve filenames

CoPilot stages File and list[File] inputs at extensionless paths
(/var/inputs/<var> for a single File, /var/inputs/<var>/<index> for
list elements), which breaks tools that sniff format by extension —
e.g. salmon rejects a gzipped FASTQ staged as "0" ("has extension ,
neither a fasta nor a fastq").

Add an opt-in DataLoadingConfig.file_input_layout enum
{DIRECT=0 (default) | NAMED_DIR=1}. DIRECT is the existing behavior,
so raw ContainerTasks are unaffected. Under NAMED_DIR the downloader
stages each File input into a per-input directory under its ORIGINAL
basename (recovered from the blob URI, which the SDK preserves on
upload), so names and extensions round-trip end-to-end:

  fasta : File        -> /var/inputs/fasta/genome.fasta
  reads : list[File]  -> /var/inputs/reads/sample_R1.fastq.gz
                         /var/inputs/reads/sample_R2.fastq.gz

list[File] elements that share a basename are de-duplicated with an
index prefix (1_reads.fastq.gz) so colliding names never clobber.
Dir inputs are multipart blobs and are untouched by the flag.

Consumers glob /var/inputs/<var>/* to read File/list[File] inputs.

- flyteidl2/core/tasks.proto: add FileInputLayout enum +
  DataLoadingConfig.file_input_layout field; regenerate Go bindings
- flytecopilot/data/download.go: per-input-dir staging under NAMED_DIR
  for single File and list[File], with basename collision dedup
- flytecopilot/cmd/download.go: --file-input-layout flag (empty=DIRECT)
- flyteplugins/.../flytek8s/copilot.go: thread pilot.GetFileInputLayout()
  into the downloader's --file-input-layout arg
- tests updated across data/, cmd/, and flytek8s/ for the new behavior

docs: Add clarification on required Kafka version field in cloud_events configuration for FlyteAdmin

The current documentation for the FlyteAdmin cloudEvents Kafka configuration does not mention that the `version` field under the `kafka` block is required. 

If this field is omitted, attempting to start FlyteAdmin with Kafka cloud events enabled leads to a panic error with the message "caught panic: invalid version".

An example of a minimal valid configuration is as follows:
```
cloudEvents:
  enable: true
  kafka:
    brokers: 127.0.0.1:9092
    version: my-kafka-version
  eventsPublisher:
    eventTypes:
      - all
    topicName: myTopic
  type: kafka
```
This change aims to help users avoid runtime errors and improve the ease of adoption for this feature.

fix(copilot): bound concurrent file uploads to keep the uploader within its memory limit

The uploader started one upload per file of a directory output, all at
once. Since stow v0.5.0 (#8115) the S3 backend uploads through the
aws-sdk-go-v2 transfer manager, which reads each body up to its 16 MiB
multipart threshold into memory, so a directory of a few hundred files
(~27 MB) now holds all of it in memory together and the sidecar is
OOMKilled at its default 128Mi.

Uploads now wait on one semaphore, shared across every output, that
allows 8 files in flight at a time.

fix(runs): honor Offset in ListActions so WatchActions returns all actions

ListActions supports keyset (CursorToken) pagination but silently ignored the
Offset field of ListResourceInput — it emitted LIMIT with no OFFSET. WatchActions'
initial full listing (listAndSendAllActions) paginates by Offset, so every page
re-read the same first ~Limit rows: a run with 1,000 actions only ever streamed
the first ~100 to the client.

Emit `OFFSET ?` when input.Offset > 0 (mutually exclusive with CursorToken, per
ListResourceInput). Cursor-based callers pass Offset=0 and are unaffected.

Adds TestListActions_OffsetPagination (order-independent count assertions that
fail on the old offset-ignored behavior).

Bind app inputs to a pinned artifact version, and list apps by consumed artifact (#7808)

App inputs could reference an artifact two ways: `artifact_query`, resolved
server-side at some unspecified time, and `artifact_id`, an `ArtifactID` whose
version was optional.

Both were the wrong shape for what apps need. An app input has to name one
exact artifact version: the client resolves the artifact at deploy time and the
app runs against that version until it is redeployed. A query that the server
re-resolves later, or an ID with the version left off, both describe a moving
reference the app can silently drift across.

Replace them with a single `artifact_id` of type `ArtifactVersionId`, which
carries the version as a required part of its identity. The field is recorded
for lineage: the server does not resolve or validate it.

Both fields were declared in #7715 and never implemented -- no server ever read
them and no client ever set them -- so they are removed outright rather than
reserved. The new field takes 6 rather than reusing 3 or 4, so the numbers that
did ship are not given a new meaning.

Also add `ConsumedArtifactFilter` to app `ListRequest`, so callers can ask which
apps consume a given artifact -- the reverse of the lineage the pinned id
records. An empty version matches any version.

Rework local-run data path onto existing dataproxy APIs

Local runs no longer get dedicated dataproxy RPCs. Uploads use
CreateUploadLocation and reads use GetActionData/CreateDownloadLink,
routed like every other data operation: the client asks
ClusterService.SelectCluster (new OPERATION_LOCAL_RUN_DATA) and the
server answers with a dataplane endpoint when the org's clusters are
directly reachable, or its own endpoint otherwise — in which case the
control plane serves the artifacts from its own storage.

Two small extensions to existing messages make this routable:
- SelectClusterResponse.cluster names the selected cluster so reporters
  can stamp it on the action attempt; reads later route by the recorded
  attempt cluster (empty = control-plane storage).
- GetActionDataRequest.run_source disambiguates resolution: run names
  are not unique across platform and local runs, so RUN_SOURCE_LOCAL
  resolves the action via LocalRunService.

Removes UploadMetadata, GetLocalActionData, CreateLocalDownloadLink and
their request messages, and the INPUTS/OUTPUTS artifact types that only
they used.

Only copy branch node outputs if expected (#676)

## Overview
https://linear.app/unionai/issue/COR-2576/branch-child-should-not-reuse-branch-data-dir-and-output-dir fixed a bug where we were repurposing the output dir, leading to races on data availability. However, once moving to explicit dirs and a copy, we introduced a bug where try and fail to copy a subworflow's output when there is none.

~This change only copies workflow node outputs (launch plan, subworkflow) when outputs are expected based on the interface.~

~Open question: I continue assuming that all other node types have outputs. It's not clear yet to me if this is a safe assumption (probably not?), but I need to gain confidence in looking up whether each node type has outputs (and future node types I guess...)~

This change ignores not found errors when copying branch node child outputs to branch node output. The assumption here is that failure to write the child branch node output should have already resulted in a failure and not found is safe to ignore.

Repro
```
import flytekit as fl
from flytekit.core.task import Echo

echo = Echo(name="echo")

@fl.task
def t1():
    pass

@fl.workflow
def sub():
    t1()

@fl.workflow
def cond_wf(val: str):
    _ = (
        fl.conditional("conditional")
        .if_(val != "")
        .then(
            sub()
        )
        .else_()
        .then(echo())
    )
```

gpufault: classify distributed child-pod faults and verify event node provenance (#7913)

* feat(executor): classify GPU faults recorded on a CRD task's child pods

Classification so far covered tasks whose tracked resource is the Pod itself. A
RayJob, PyTorchJob, MPIJob or TFJob records the Xid on a worker pod while the
executor tracks the CRD, so the fault the node saw never reached the failure the
user read, and a GPU that fell off the bus during distributed training still
looked like the workload's own crash.

Nothing new has to be watched to fix that. The event informer is not scoped to
the tracked resource, so a worker pod's events are already cached, and the Pod
informer is already running and already selects on the managed label that every
plugin merges into the pod templates it builds. What was missing was a way to
name the pods: an operator's child pod names carry a random suffix, so the
executor cannot derive the keys the events are cached under.

ChildPodDiscovery is the optional interface that closes that, in the shape
PluginAbortOverride already established. A plugin returns the label selector that
picks out this attempt's pods; the manager lists them from the resource's own
namespace out of the cache it already holds, and reads each one's faults. Because
the pods arrive as objects, their UIDs are known, so the identity check that
already guarded the Pod path applies unchanged and never has to fall back to
matching on a name.

AttemptPodSelector builds the half of that selector which holds whichever
operator created the pod. The run, action and attempt labels move to flytek8s
next to the managed label, for the reason that one already lives there: the
plugins that build pod templates have to keep them intact. It refuses to build a
selector when any of them is missing, since run and action are dropped when
sanitization empties them and selecting on what is left would reach another
action's pods. PreservedPodLabels exposes the same key set for plugins to
re-apply after any labels a user supplied, so that the two halves cannot disagree
about which labels have to survive.

Which pods are consulted is narrower than everything the selector matches. A
worker that finished its work cannot be why the job failed, so a succeeded pod
contributes nothing even if it logged a fault mid-run; crediting that to a
launcher's user-code failure would turn a user error into a hardware one and stop
charging the retry. A pod still running is kept, because a worker wedged on a GPU
that fell off the bus is exactly the case this path exists for.

Relevance is anchored per pod on that pod's own container termination, because
every CRD plugin stamps the failure with the time of the reconcile that noticed
it rather than with anything the kubelet recorded, and anchoring on the reconcile
would age out a fault that killed a worker minutes earlier. Init containers are
not eligible anchors: they finish before the workload starts, and a native
sidecar declared among them is reaped after everything else. The anchor is never
later than the attempt's own failure, so a pod torn down long afterwards cannot
let faults recorded in the meantime explain it.

Which fault wins needs no new rule: ClassifyFailure already takes the worst
severity and the earliest within it, so the faults gathered across pods are only
sorted back into order before being handed over. That order is on when each fault
was first recorded rather than when it was last seen, because a fault that is
still repeating has a later last observation than a one-shot fault that followed
it, and ordering on that would let a downstream symptom outrank the root cause.
The last observation still decides relevance, which is all it was ever for.

The one pod whose fault settled the verdict is named as an additional reason,
because the fault sentence carries the Xid, the GPU and the node but not the pod,
which on a job with sixty-four workers is not enough to act on. Only that pod is
named: pointing at every pod that saw any fault would put a misleading reason on
a failure the faults did not explain, and would emit one cluster event per pod
when a whole node's worth of GPUs faults at once. The single pod path names
nothing, since the failure is already reported against that pod.

A gang-scheduled restart creates fresh pods under the same attempt and its faults
count, while an earlier Flyte attempt's pods are excluded by the attempt label. A
plugin that does not implement the interface contributes no pods and so no
faults, which is exactly what it did before.

A pod already torn down with its job is not recovered. The events are cached
under a name nothing can reconstruct, so discovery logs at debug and classifies
nothing rather than guessing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Samhita Alla <aallasamhita@gmail.com>

* feat(ray,kfoperators,clustered): name the child pods of a distributed task

The Ray, Kubeflow and clustered plugins track a CRD, so they implement
ChildPodDiscovery to tell the framework where the pods that actually ran the task
are.

All three build the same selector: the attempt's own labels, which the pod
templates they hand the operator already carry, narrowed by one label the
operator applies to the pods themselves. For Kubeflow that is
training.kubeflow.org/job-name, which is the CR's own name and so is known from
the moment the resource exists; one implementation in common covers PyTorchJob,
MPIJob and TFJob, because all three get their replica pods from the same
operator. For the clustered plugin it is jobset.sigs.k8s.io/jobset-name, exported
by the vendored JobSet API the plugin already imports. For Ray it is
ray.io/cluster, which KubeRay stamps on head and worker pods and overwrites on
the template, and whose value is only knowable from the RayJob's status because
KubeRay appends a random suffix to the cluster name.

Until that status is reported Ray falls back to the attempt labels alone. That is
not a wider search in any sense that matters, since run, action and attempt
already pin the selector to one attempt of one action; the most it can add is the
job submitter pod, which has no GPU and so no faults to contribute. The
alternative, declining until the operator catches up, would lose the fault on
exactly the runs where the cluster never came up healthy.

Ray also has to stop a task from taking its own pods out of reach. The head and
worker templates let a task supply k8s_pod metadata, and that metadata was
unioned after the execution labels with only the managed label re-forced
afterwards, so a user label named run, action or attempt would overwrite the
identity the selector looks a pod up by. All three templates now re-apply
flytek8s.PreservedPodLabels last, which is the same key set the selector is built
from. Dask and Spark are left for a follow-up.

The conformance tests are the point of the test additions. Each asserts that the
labels the plugin puts on the pod templates satisfy the selector the same plugin
hands the framework, for every replica type it builds. The two halves live far
apart and drift on either one would leave a GPU fault on a worker silently
unclassified, which is the failure mode this whole path exists to prevent.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Samhita Alla <aallasamhita@gmail.com>

* fix(executor): stop excluding and mis-naming the pods a GPU fault came from

Three things the executor decided about child pods were wrong.

The gate deciding whether to name the pod a fault was found on asked whether the
failure carried one of the gpufault codes, and it never opened on a real task.
ClassifyFailure only replaces a code the plugin had no opinion about, and the CRD
plugins all report codes of their own: ray reports TaskFailedWithError, kubeflow
DownstreamSystemError, clustered a JobSet condition reason. Those are exactly the
codes it is right to keep, so every distributed GPU failure lost the one line
saying which worker the hardware failed on. What actually says a fault was folded
in is the fault itself, which ClassifyFailure puts on the error in every case it
acts, so the gate reads that now and returns early only for a warning, which rides
along as data without deciding anything. Finding the pod still matches the settled
fault back by pointer, so it rests on ClassifyFailure passing the same fault
through rather than a copy; that invariant now has a test, and failing to find the
pod is logged rather than passed over, so breaking it cannot cost that line again
unnoticed.

Deciding a worker had finished by looking at all its containers called a pod
unfinished forever when a sidecar held it open, which is what a legacy-injected
service mesh proxy does: the work exits cleanly, the proxy never does, and a
faulting worker was excluded from classification for the life of the pod. What
settles it is the container running the task's own work, so that is what is asked
about now. Only a declared primary counts, through the new
DeclaredPrimaryContainerName, which reads the annotations and nothing else.
GetPrimaryContainerName cannot answer this: it falls back to guessing the first
container, and the container it picks may be the sidecar. Where nobody declared a
primary the older rule still stands.

The bound on a child pod's anchor was skipped when the plugin reported no failure
time of its own, on the reasoning that there was nothing to bound against. There
is: a pod the operator has not finished tearing down then anchored at the moment
of the reconcile and swept in every fault the node had recorded since. Now stands
in, which is what PodFailureTime already falls back to, so the two agree.

PreservedPodLabels also gains the task name. It takes no part in selection and is
deliberately absent from the selector's keys, but the per-pod metrics external
collectors scrape are joined on it, and a user label of the same name would point
those joins at the wrong task. The preserved set and the selection set are no
longer the same list, so each names its own keys and says why they differ.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Samhita Alla <aallasamhita@gmail.com>

* fix(ray,clustered,kfoperators): select the right child pods, and only those

Ray never stamped TaskInfo.OccurredAt, so the framework had no failure time for a
Ray task at all. Everything measured against it degraded: a GPU fault's relevance,
and the bound on a child pod's own anchor, which was skipped entirely for want of
anything to bound against. It now stamps the reconcile time the way every other
CRD plugin does.

Ray's fallback when the cluster name was not yet known selected on the attempt
labels alone, on the reasoning that those are exact to one attempt of one action.
They are not: they are sanitized and truncated to the 63 characters a label value
allows, so two long action names sharing a prefix collapse onto one value and
another action's pods would answer for this one. The fallback bought nothing to
weigh against that, because KubeRay fills the cluster name in before it creates the
RayCluster, so an empty one means no pod exists yet and there is nothing on record
to find. It now looks at nothing, and the comment says why instead of repeating the
claim that truncation breaks.

The clustered plugin selected every generation of a restarted JobSet at once. A
restart recreates every child pod under the same JobSet name, so name alone pooled
the pods of every generation the attempt had been through and let a fault from one
that died half an hour ago explain the failure of the one running now. The
selector now also carries the restart generation, which the JobSet controller
stamps on the pods it creates and which Status.Restarts holds for the generation
now running: exhausting the restart budget is what ends the attempt, and it does
not increment on the way out. While a restart is in flight the two disagree for an
instant and the selector matches nothing, which is the direction to fail in.

All three plugins now also name the container running the task's own work on the
pod templates they build, which is what lets the executor tell that work from a
sidecar that outlives it. Ray knows it for the head and the worker; the clustered
plugin already had it in hand for the JobSet; kubeflow's replica containers are
renamed to the operator's own fixed name by the webhook, which ToReplicaSpec has
just applied, so it is the same name for every replica role.

Signed-off-by: Samhita Alla <aallasamhita@gmail.com>

* fix(executor): carry a failed attempt's reasons through an in-place restart

An in-place restart replaces the failure with a Queued phase so the TaskAction
stays non-terminal. The replacement was built from nothing, so the reasons the
failed attempt had accumulated went with it, and on this path they are the only
account of what happened that ever reaches the user: the failure itself is
discarded and never reported. For a GPU fault that means the line naming which
worker the hardware failed on was written and then thrown away, leaving a task
that appears to have restarted for no reason.

queuedForInPlaceRestart carries the reasons across and nothing else. The rest of
the failed attempt's task info stays behind on purpose, because its logs and custom
info describe the pod that has just been deleted rather than the one being queued.
Naming the conversion also gives it somewhere to be tested, which the path it is
inlined in does not have without an API server.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Samhita Alla <aallasamhita@gmail.com>

* fix(flytek8s): the framework's primary-container stamp outranks kubectl's

DeclaredPrimaryContainerName read kubectl.kubernetes.io/default-container
ahead of the annotation the plugins stamp at build time. That let a pod
template pointing kubectl at a sidecar decide which container's exit
settles GPU fault classification: a sidecar exiting cleanly would mark
the pod succeeded while the real workload was still wedged, losing the
fault. Flyte's own stamp now wins; the kubectl annotation still answers
for pods the framework never stamped, where a declaration beats a guess.

* fix(flytek8s): preserve the managed label only when the task carries it

A framework that runs these plugins without the executor's Pod cache doesn't mark its
tasks as managed, so its pods should not claim to be. The executor always stamps the
label on task metadata, so its pods keep it.

* gpufault: trust a pod's fault event only from its own node (#8153)

# Why

A GPU fault event is only worth believing when the fault emitter on the pod's own node wrote it. The emitter's credentials only let it record events for its own node, so an event reported from any other node did not come from the emitter watching the pod's GPUs. The executor's failure classifier checked the event reason and the regarding UID, but not the reporting node, and its event watcher did not record the reporting node at all. A consumer that wanted a typed fault for an attached pod event had to parse the free-text message, with none of these checks.

# What

- gpufault gains trust.go. FromPodEvent(PodEvent, Pod) returns the typed fault only for a trusted event: a GPUXidError or GPUSXidError reason, recorded against this very pod, and reported from the pod's node. The trade the classifier already made stays and is documented: when the pod is gone and only its name is left, the name match is accepted. A pod with a UID but no node was never scheduled and has no trusted faults. IsFaultReason is exported for callers that filter before logging.
- pluginsCore.ReasonInfo gains GpuFault, set only for an event that passed FromPodEvent.
- The executor's event watcher records the reporting node of each event: reportingInstance, else the deprecated source host.
- classifyGpuFailure uses FromPodEvent for its per-event checks, so a fault reported from another node no longer reclassifies a failure. RelevantToFailure still bounds the search in time.
- The executor sets ReasonInfo.GpuFault on the pod events it attaches to a phase, and toClusterEvents copies it onto ClusterEvent.gpu\_fault. The message is never parsed for a fault there.

# Tests

- New table in gpufault/trust\_test.go covering each rule and each trade, a wrong reason with a valid-looking message, and an SXid.
- plugin\_manager\_test: a fault reported from another node does not classify, and attached reasons carry a fault only when trusted. event\_watcher\_test: the reporting node is recorded and survives aggregation.
- go test -race passes for gpufault, pluginmachinery/core and executor/pkg/plugin/k8s, and the lint diff against main is clean. The new toClusterEvents spec is in the controller's Ginkgo suite, which needs envtest binaries and was not run locally.

A downstream consumer that tags faults on pod events switches to FromPodEvent once this lands.

Show non-PgError errors when connecting to db (#445)

Signed-off-by: Sam Lai <70988+slai@users.noreply.github.com>

When connecting to a database instance that doesn't exist, that error is currently masked due to an invalid assumption that all wrapped errors returned from gorm are of type `*pgconn.PgError`. When a network error occurs, the returned error is of type `*net.OpError`. This causes the following panic -

```
{"json":{"src":"base.go:73"},"level":"fatal","msg":"caught panic: interface conversion: error is *net.OpError, not *pgconn.PgError [goroutine 1 [running]:\nruntime/debug.Stack()\n\t/home/user/.local/go/src/runtime/debug/stack.go:24
...
```

... and doesn't show what the actual error is.

This PR fixes that by using the functions in the `errors` package to check if the error chain contains an error of type `*pgconn.PgError`, and if not, simply returns the error.

It also removes the ConnectError interface, as it is no longer needed - the `errors.As` function will automatically check the whole error chain and unwrap as necessary.

With this fix, the error becomes -

```
{"json":{"src":"base.go:82"},"level":"fatal","msg":"failed to connect to `host=localhost user=postgres database=flyte`: dial error (dial tcp 127.0.0.1:5432: connect: connection refused)","ts":"2022-06-11T20:48:28+01:00"}
```

fix(actions): record on DELETE so create-then-delete actions aren't lost

A TaskAction created and deleted before the worker processes its coalesced
ADDED event was never recorded: handleWatchEvent reads the latest from the
cache, finds it already gone (getLatest -> !found), and bails without calling
RecordAction. The subsequent DELETE only issued a terminal UpdateActionStatus,
which matched 0 rows because no row existed, silently dropping the action.

Fix: notifyRunService now records on every event type (including DELETED),
deduplicated via the recordedFilter. The DELETE tombstone still carries Spec,
so recording from it creates the row before the terminal update. The dedup
filter is now mandatory (NewActionsClient returns an error if it can't be
built, falling back to a default size), which keeps the record path idempotent
across the normal lifecycle. Parent-promotion is gated to non-DELETED events so
a tearing-down child doesn't re-drive its parent's phase.

Tests: add create-then-delete (DELETE records + terminates) and DELETE-after-record
(no double record); drop the obsolete nil-filter test now that the filter is mandatory.

feat(flytestdlib): route redis:// references via scheme when redis.addr is set

When storage is configured with a non-redis type plus redis.addr, wrap
the raw store in a scheme router: redis:// references dispatch to a
RedisStore, everything else to the configured store. This lets metadata
(inputs/outputs protobufs, via a redis:// metadata bucket prefix) live
in Redis while raw data, code-bundle signed URLs, and all other IO keep
using the blob store. Activated purely by the reference scheme - no
behavior change unless redis:// paths are used.

CopyRaw on the router reuses copyImpl pointed at the router itself, so
cross-backend copies (redis <-> blob store) work through plain
ReadRaw/WriteRaw.

fix(runs): size watch subscriber channels from watchBufferSize

The runs service's watchBufferSize setting was declared but never read: every
WatchRunUpdates, WatchAllRunUpdates, WatchAllActionUpdates and
WatchActionUpdates subscriber got a fixed 100-slot channel, and
processNotifications drops a notification for a subscriber whose channel is
full. A client watching a parent through a burst of hundreds of children
finishing could lose the parent's own terminal update and wait forever, and
raising runs.watchBufferSize didn't help.

Carry WatchBufferSize into the repository's NotificationConfig and size the
four subscriber channels from it. Zero or below keeps today's 100.

fix(cache): refresh entries older than maxCacheAge instead of missing again (#8204)

fix(cache): replace entries older than maxCacheAge on Put

With catalogCache.maxCacheAge set, Get treats an entry older than that
as a miss and the task runs again. The cache client's Put never sent
max_age, and the cache service only replaces an existing entry when the
request sets overwrite or carries an expired max_age. It answered
AlreadyExists, the stale entry kept its old last-updated time, and
every later run missed the cache again. Send max_age on Put and Update
when maxCacheAge is set.

storage: bump stow to v0.5.0, pass the context to stow

stow v0.5.0 moves its S3 provider to aws-sdk-go-v2, so the errors it
returns are smithy errors and no longer awserr.Error. The checks for a
missing bucket and for a bucket the caller already owns matched on
awserr.Error and would silently stop matching: a write to a missing
bucket would not create it, and creating an existing bucket would

feat: scope executor informer cache to flyte-managed pods

controller-runtime caches every watched object across all namespaces, so
the executor holds every Pod in the cluster. On a large multi-tenant
cluster that is several GB of resident memory and OOMKills the executor.

Label every Pod the executor is responsible for with flyte.org/managed
and select on it in the manager cache.

The label is injected once, in NewTaskExecutionMetadata. Every k8s plugin
merges the TaskExecutionMetadata labels into the object it builds, so a
single injection point covers all of them: the plain pod plugin through
addObjectMetadata, Ray head/worker/submitter, Kubeflow replicas and Spark
driver/executor through the Pod templates embedded in their CRDs, and
Dask through the CRD metadata its operator copies onto the scheduler,
worker and job-runner Pods.

The label is unioned last in each of those merges, so neither platform
defaults nor user-supplied labels can drop it. The Ray plugin applies a
task's k8s_pod metadata after the execution labels, so the label is
reapplied there to keep a task from hiding its own head and worker Pods.
Losing the label would make a Pod invisible to the executor that created
it, which checkResourcePhase would then report as deleted externally.

The constants live in flytek8s rather than the executor because the
plugins that build Pod templates have to keep the label intact.

Closes #7831

Implement a recursive finalize in node executor (#30)

Implement Finalize in Dynamic Node Handler.
The change is more nuanced than this. It changes how Dynamic Nodes fail.

- When a sub-node in a dynamic node fails, the dynamic node will continue to be marked as `Running` in this cycle but change its internal phase to `failing`
- Next cycle, the dynamic node will abort all other sub-nodes that are still running then mark itself as `retryable failure`

fix(ray,clustered,kfoperators): select the right child pods, and only those

Ray never stamped TaskInfo.OccurredAt, so the framework had no failure time for a
Ray task at all. Everything measured against it degraded: a GPU fault's relevance,
and the bound on a child pod's own anchor, which was skipped entirely for want of
anything to bound against. It now stamps the reconcile time the way every other
CRD plugin does.

Ray's fallback when the cluster name was not yet known selected on the attempt
labels alone, on the reasoning that those are exact to one attempt of one action.
They are not: they are sanitized and truncated to the 63 characters a label value
allows, so two long action names sharing a prefix collapse onto one value and
another action's pods would answer for this one. The fallback bought nothing to
weigh against that, because KubeRay fills the cluster name in before it creates the
RayCluster, so an empty one means no pod exists yet and there is nothing on record
to find. It now looks at nothing, and the comment says why instead of repeating the
claim that truncation breaks.

The clustered plugin selected every generation of a restarted JobSet at once. A
restart recreates every child pod under the same JobSet name, so name alone pooled
the pods of every generation the attempt had been through and let a fault from one
that died half an hour ago explain the failure of the one running now. The
selector now also carries the restart generation, which the JobSet controller
stamps on the pods it creates and which Status.Restarts holds for the generation
now running: exhausting the restart budget is what ends the attempt, and it does
not increment on the way out. While a restart is in flight the two disagree for an
instant and the selector matches nothing, which is the direction to fail in.

All three plugins now also name the container running the task's own work on the
pod templates they build, which is what lets the executor tell that work from a
sidecar that outlives it. Ray knows it for the head and the worker; the clustered
plugin already had it in hand for the JobSet; kubeflow's replica containers are
renamed to the operator's own fixed name by the webhook, which ToReplicaSpec has
just applied, so it is the same name for every replica role.

chore(flyte-binary): remove dead self-hosted auth config

The v2 binary has no self-hosted OAuth2 authorization server. It registers no
'auth' config section; runs/config reads only authMetadata.* (external/delegated
auth) and advertises a public client via authMetadata.flyteClient.

So the chart's '014-auth-secrets.yaml' rendering (auth.appAuth.selfAuthServer.
staticClients) was never consumed, and with it gone the entire configuration.auth
block in values.yaml (oidc, internal, flyteClient, authorizedUris,
clientSecretsExternalSecretRef, enable* gates) is dead. Remove both and replace
the values block with a pointer to flyte-core-components.runs.authMetadata.

helm template output is unchanged for default values, and the selfAuthServer
secret no longer renders even when the old auth.* values are forced on.

This change updates `FutureFileReader.Cache` and `FutureFileReader.RetrieveCache` to use overlapped write and reads, respectively, to reduce end-to-end latency. fix: pin docker-registry haSharedSecret to avoid sandbox manifest churn (#7108)

The docker-registry Helm subchart generates a random haSharedSecret on
every helm template run when the value is not set. This causes
complete.yaml and dev.yaml to always show as modified after running
`make sandbox-build`, even with no actual deployment changes.

Pin the secret to a static value in flyte-sandbox values.yaml since this
is a local development sandbox environment.

Webhook: serve extra mutators and port v1 secret-injection fixes

The executor's pod webhook only ever served the secrets mutator. Deployments
that embed it (Union's single-binary onebox, and eventually its data plane in
place of the flytepropeller v1 webhook) need to add their own pod and node
mutators, and need the fixes the v1 webhook accumulated.

Handlers:
- PodMutator / NodeMutator interfaces and a generic handler; each mutator is
  its own MutatingWebhook with its own path (/mutate--v1-<kind>/<id>), name
  and object selector.
- Setup/NewWebhook take options: WithPodMutators, WithNodeMutators,
  WithHandlers (custom name/paths), WithLimitNamespace.
- The secrets handler keeps /mutate--v1-pod and is also served at
  /mutate--v1-pod/secrets, the path charts that render the configuration
  themselves use. webhookTimeout is applied to every webhook.

Secrets (ported from the v1 webhook):
- clusterName and the cluster-scoped eager API key lookup.
- The image-pull Secret informer is only started when needed and is scoped
  to the limit namespace.
- InitCerts keeps a valid existing cert Secret instead of regenerating on
  every start (which churned the CA bundle under running replicas).

feat(flytestdlib): add redis-backed storage to the storage module

Adds a "redis" storage type alongside the stow-backed and in-memory raw
stores, letting run metadata (inputs/outputs protobufs) live in Redis
instead of an object store. Objects are stored as plain Redis string
values keyed by the path portion of the DataReference
(redis://<addr>/<key>), with directories emulated as key prefixes via
SCAN. This path model matches the flyte-sdk redis plugin
(flyteorg/flyte-sdk#1191), so references written by one side resolve on
the other.

Selected with `storage: { type: redis, redis: { addr: host:port } }`;
username/password/db are optional. List is paginated by mapping the
storage Cursor onto the Redis SCAN cursor; ReadRaw enforces the
existing maxDownloadMBs limit; signed URLs are unsupported. Tests run
against miniredis (new test-only dependency) and cover raw IO round
trips, empty values, Head/Delete/List pagination, the download limit,
and end-to-end DataStore usage including reference construction and
CopyRaw.

adding execution specific env vars to actors (#659)

## Overview
This PR adds execution specific environment variables to actors, which allows retrieving task / node / execution IDs (among other metadata) within the `actor.task` function executions.

## Test Plan
This was tested locally.

```
from flytekit import current_context, workflow
from union.actor import ActorEnvironment


actor_env = ActorEnvironment(
    name="penguin0",
    replica_count=1,
    ttl_seconds=30,
    container_image="hamersaw/penguin:v0",
)


@actor_env.task
def say_hello(name: str) -> str:
    import os
    pod_name = os.environ.get('_F_PN')
    run_name = current_context().execution_id.name
    return f"hello {name} {pod_name} {run_name}"


@workflow
def say_hello_wf(name: str) -> str:
    return say_hello(name=name)
```

Accept OIDC ID tokens presented with the Bearer scheme

flyteadmin already accepts an ID token from its userAuth OIDC provider over
gRPC when the client sends it with the IDToken scheme, which is how the
console authenticates. Some clients can only send Bearer: flytectl's
ExternalCommand auth type and flytekit's external_process mode hardcode
that scheme. Today such a token fails access-token validation against the
authorization server and the request is rejected, even though flyteadmin
could have verified it as an ID token.

When a Bearer token fails validation as an access token and is not
accompanied by an IDToken-scheme token, try it as an ID token from the
userAuth provider before rejecting the request, on both the gRPC
interceptor and the HTTP path. Verification is identical to the IDToken
scheme: signature, issuer, audience (the userAuth client id) and expiry
through go-oidc. Tokens that fail as both are rejected as before, with the
ID token error added to the message.

This lets a host without a browser log in through the provider's device
flow and hand the ID token to a stock flytectl via ExternalCommand. It is
the server-side complement to #8080, which teaches the client to send the
IDToken scheme itself.

fix(executor): stop excluding and mis-naming the pods a GPU fault came from

Three things the executor decided about child pods were wrong.

The gate deciding whether to name the pod a fault was found on asked whether the
failure carried one of the gpufault codes, and it never opened on a real task.
ClassifyFailure only replaces a code the plugin had no opinion about, and the CRD
plugins all report codes of their own: ray reports TaskFailedWithError, kubeflow
DownstreamSystemError, clustered a JobSet condition reason. Those are exactly the
codes it is right to keep, so every distributed GPU failure lost the one line
saying which worker the hardware failed on. What actually says a fault was folded
in is the fault itself, which ClassifyFailure puts on the error in every case it
acts, so the gate reads that now and returns early only for a warning, which rides
along as data without deciding anything. Finding the pod still matches the settled
fault back by pointer, so it rests on ClassifyFailure passing the same fault
through rather than a copy; that invariant now has a test, and failing to find the
pod is logged rather than passed over, so breaking it cannot cost that line again
unnoticed.

Deciding a worker had finished by looking at all its containers called a pod
unfinished forever when a sidecar held it open, which is what a legacy-injected
service mesh proxy does: the work exits cleanly, the proxy never does, and a
faulting worker was excluded from classification for the life of the pod. What
settles it is the container running the task's own work, so that is what is asked
about now. Only a declared primary counts, through the new
DeclaredPrimaryContainerName, which reads the annotations and nothing else.
GetPrimaryContainerName cannot answer this: it falls back to guessing the first
container, and the container it picks may be the sidecar. Where nobody declared a
primary the older rule still stands.

The bound on a child pod's anchor was skipped when the plugin reported no failure
time of its own, on the reasoning that there was nothing to bound against. There
is: a pod the operator has not finished tearing down then anchored at the moment
of the reconcile and swept in every fault the node had recorded since. Now stands
in, which is what PodFailureTime already falls back to, so the two agree.

PreservedPodLabels also gains the task name. It takes no part in selection and is
deliberately absent from the selector's keys, but the per-pod metrics external
collectors scrape are joined on it, and a user label of the same name would point
those joins at the wrong task. The preserved set and the selection set are no
longer the same list, so each names its own keys and says why they differ.

feat(secret): invalidate webhook secret cache on write

The pod webhook's embedded secret manager caches resolved secret values,
so a secret written through SecretService was not visible to task pods
until the cache TTL expired. Have every write path (create, update,
delete) drop the cached copy immediately.

lookUpSecret caches under whichever cascade scope the fetcher resolved
at, so invalidation clears all three keys (project+domain, domain, org).
Clearing only the exact tuple would leave a shadowing broader-scope entry
behind and the cascade would keep serving the stale value. Create is a
write for the same reason: a new narrow-scope secret can be shadowed by
an already-cached broader-scope one.

The secret service and the webhook run in the same process in the
unified binary, so this is a direct call — no invalidation endpoint or
service fanout. SecretCacheInvalidator is nil in the standalone
secret-service binary, where invalidation is a no-op.

[Bug] Update resource failures w/ Finalizers set  (#423) (#5673)

## Overview
when [informer cache has stale values](https://github.com/unionai/flyte/blob/1e82352dd95f89630e333fe6105d5fdb5487a24e/flytepropeller/pkg/controller/nodes/task/k8s/plugin_manager.go#L478), we cannot update the k8s resource when [clearing finalizers](https://github.com/unionai/flyte/blob/1e82352dd95f89630e333fe6105d5fdb5487a24e/flytepropeller/pkg/controller/nodes/task/k8s/plugin_manager.go#L450) and get `Error: Operation cannot be fulfilled on pods.` The current implementation bubbles up the error resulting in a system retry. By the next loop, the informer cache is up to date and the update is able to be applied. However, in an ArrayNode with many subnodes getting executed in parallel, the execution can easily run out of retries.

This update adds a basic retry with exponential backoff to wait for the informer cache to get up to date.

## Test Plan
Ran in dogfood-gcp
- https://buildkite.com/unionai/managed-cluster-staging-sync/builds/4622 + manually updated configmap to enabled finalizers

- Run with change (https://dogfood-gcp.cloud-staging.union.ai/console/projects/flytesnacks/domains/development/executions/f016a3be7fa304db5a77/nodeId/n0/nodes)

feat(sentry): count deploy_task, deploy_app and deploy_trigger server-side

Only CreateRun was instrumented, so the flyte.operation counter measured
runs and nothing else. flyte-sdk already emits deploy_task, deploy_app
and deploy_trigger for the same metric, which means counting them here
too makes the OSS share of each operation observable: subtract the OSS
count from the SDK count and what is left ran against a non-OSS backend.

Move the Sentry wiring out of runs/setup.go into flytestdlib/sentryutils
so the app service can share it, and take a procedure -> operation map
instead of hardcoding CreateRun. Attach the interceptor to the Task and
Trigger handlers, and to AppService.

Triggers declared on a task ride along inside DeployTaskRequest, so
TriggerService.DeployTrigger only ever sees standalone deploys; count
the triggers carried by DeployTask as well or deploy_trigger reports
close to zero.

Move settings desc field option off extension number 50000

The desc field option on google.protobuf.FieldOptions sat at 50000, in
the range protobuf reserves for internal use within a single
organization. That range is only safe when you control every .proto
sharing a descriptor pool. flyteidl2 is published to buf.build, PyPI and
npm, so it routinely shares a pool with third-party protos, and desc
collided with another published extension claiming the same tag. The
collision fails extension registration at import time for anyone
importing both schemas.

Move desc to 1364, from a block of 1364-1373 requested for Flyte in the
protobuf global extension registry
(protocolbuffers/protobuf#29013). The block deliberately starts after
1314-1363, which is claimed by the currently open
protocolbuffers/protobuf#28919.

This is backwards compatible. desc is a descriptor-level annotation
living in FieldOptions, so it is never serialized into any RPC payload,
and every consumer references the generated symbol rather than the
literal number. The only fallout is transient and cosmetic: during
version skew, a mixed-version reader of a serialized FileDescriptorProto
drops the annotation as an unknown field.

Also correct the usage docblock, which referenced the org package and
org.E_Desc. The extension lives in flyteidl2.settings and generates as
settings.E_Desc.

fix(executor): drop event watcher cache buckets when their last event goes

objectCache kept a bucket for every (namespace, name, kind) it ever saw an
event for. OnDelete removed the event from the bucket but deliberately left
the bucket itself behind, to avoid racing a concurrent store against the
removal of the top-level map entry, and nothing else ever removed one. The
map therefore grew for the life of the process, keyed by every object the
cluster emitted an event about rather than by what the executor still cares
about. Pod names are unique per attempt, so even the Flyte-only subset never
reached a steady state.

Driving store and OnDelete for 200k distinct objects and then deleting every
event left all 200k buckets and ~116 MB resident with every inner map empty.

The bucket is now dropped when its last event is deleted, which closes the
race rather than avoiding it: the evicted flag and the map removal both
happen under the bucket's own write lock, so a store that already loaded the
bucket blocks, observes the flag and retries against a fresh one, while a
store that has not loaded it yet cannot reach it once it is out of the map.
The lock order is bucket-then-map here and map-then-bucket nowhere, since
every other path releases the map's lock before taking a bucket's, so the
two cannot deadlock. The same 200k probe now retains nothing.

This bounds objectCache to objects with a live event. It does not address
the other half of #7992, that the Event informer itself is unscoped and
caches every Event in the cluster; scoping it needs a decision about which
events the executor should watch.

ray.proto and wire it into the Ray plugin so each group's pod spec
reflects its own GPU accelerator and shared memory configuration.

and applies each group's extended resources on top of the task-level
extended resources already baked into the base pod spec. The shared
`objectMeta` is copied per group to avoid leaking group-specific labels

docs(monitoring): explain why the dashboard ships as a ConfigMap

"Can I just import it from the UI?" is the obvious question, and the answer
depends on something not visible from the Grafana UI: a UI import lives in
grafana.db under /var/lib/grafana, so it only survives a pod restart if that
path is persisted. kube-prometheus-stack ships persistence.enabled: false, so
by default it is an emptyDir and the dashboard silently disappears on the next
restart, upgrade or eviction.

Measured on a live Grafana with both kinds present: after a rollout restart the
provisioned dashboard still served and the imported one returned 404.

Documents the difference and gives the one-liner to check which case a cluster
is in, so the choice is informed rather than a matter of taste.

revert(runs): drop unverified ID-token trust; restrict enrichment to validated token

The flyte-authorization ID token header is client-controlled and not validated by
the load balancer, so decoding it without verifying the signature is an identity
spoofing vector (flagged by security review). Revert reading it. The userinfo
enricher stays the name/email source: it sends the LB-validated access token to the
IdP, which validates it and returns the real claims — no spoofing possible. Also
drop the cookie-path x-amzn-oidc-accesstoken fallback (expired by request time, only
produced 401s); the cookie path uses the proxy-signed x-amzn-oidc-data claims.

idl: restrict the character set of artifact name and version (#8092)

A (name, version) pair identifies a parent in
ArtifactSpec.parent_artifacts, and cloud stores that pair encoded into a
single scalar so it can be indexed. Today both fields carry only a max_len,
no charset, so that encoding is not injective and a lineage query can return
the wrong rows:

  name="a@v1", version="b"     -> "a@v1@b"
  name="a",    version="v1@b"  -> "a@v1@b"

Asking for the children of the first returns the second's children. That is
a wrong answer, not a slow one. Verified against Postgres 15: with a text[]
of encoded pairs both rows match; with structured comparison only the real
child does.

Restricts characters only — the pattern on the optional fields is `*`, not
`+`, so nothing that was allowed to be empty becomes required. Follows the
style already used in secret/definition.proto.

Checked against real data before choosing the set: every artifact name and
version in staging (65 versions, 10 names across five projects and three
domains) matches ^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$, so this rejects nothing that exists
there. It does constrain future values, which is the point.

artifact: parent is a full artifact reference, not a bare version (#7963)

Replaces ArtifactSpec.parent_version and ProducedArtifact.parent_version
(same field numbers — the string fields shipped in v2.0.46 but nothing
consumes them yet, so a clean break beats a reserved graveyard) with
parent_artifact, a core.ArtifactVersionId.

A bare version string could only express lineage within one artifact
name. A full reference lets a version record derivation across
artifacts — a model deriving from a dataset version — while keeping the
common same-name case as terse as before: empty key fields inherit the
child's own scope and name, so {version: "v1"} still means "the v1 of
this same artifact".

The parent must live in the artifact's own org/project/domain (same
convention as ArtifactSource provenance). Everything else is unchanged:
stored as given, never resolved, dangling parents legal, immutable
after creation. The ListArtifacts children filter becomes the
parent_name + parent_version EQUAL pair, always together, replacing the
name-scoped parent_version filter.

fix(executor): wait out RetryStrategy.backoff between user retries

#7308 added `RetryStrategy.backoff` to the protos and the SDKs serialize
it, but the executor relaunched a failed attempt on its next reconcile
regardless, so retries fired back-to-back at the requeue interval.

Stamp `Status.NextAttemptAt` when a user retry is scheduled, from both
the in-place restart and the max-runtime timeout paths, using
`min(base * factor**n, cap)` for the n-th retry as the SDKs document.
While it lies in the future the reconcile requeues for the remainder
instead of handling the plugin; it is cleared when the attempt launches.
Tasks without a backoff are unchanged.

* flyte-binary-v2: save CPU base to Depot ephemeral registry

buildx refuses local OCI export for multi-node multi-arch builds
(error: "oci for multi-node builds currently not supported"), and
Depot intentionally uses one native node per platform. Switch the
CPU build to Depot's ephemeral registry via `save: true` and a
unique per-run tag, and have the GPU build resolve `FROM` directly
from `registry.depot.dev/<project>:<tag>` — auth is implicit since
both builds run in the same Depot project. Drops the OCI tarball
extract step and the build-contexts indirection.

Refs: https://github.com/docker/buildx/discussions/2351

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* flyte-binary-v2: gate image push on `test-push-image` PR label

Lets a maintainer push test images from a PR by applying the
`test-push-image` label, and removes the temporary push: true hacks.
The gate is hoisted to a single workflow-level PUSH_IMAGES env that
all push/if checks read.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* devbox-bundled: drop security.insecure by switching preload to skopeo

The preload step ran rootless podman inside a RUN to fetch and save
image tarballs, which required `--security=insecure` and a daemon
configured with `--allow-insecure-entitlement security.insecure`.
Depot's hosted builders refuse that entitlement.

Skopeo does the same job (pull + retag + save as docker-archive) as
a privilege-free registry client, so the entitlement isn't needed
anywhere now. Drop it from the workflow steps and the local Makefile
builder config too.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* flyte-binary-v2: docker login to Depot Registry before GPU build

The GPU build's `FROM registry.depot.dev/<project>:cpu-build-...`
was 401-ing because cross-build auth in Depot's registry is not
implicit — even within the same project. Generate a short-lived
pull-token via the Depot CLI and `docker login` so the runner's
docker config (forwarded to remote BuildKit by depot/build-push-action)
can resolve the saved CPU base.

feat(runs): enrich executed_by name/email via OIDC userinfo on the Bearer path

The SDK/CLI forwards an OAuth access token that carries only the subject — profile
claims (email, given_name, family_name) live in userinfo, not the token. So on the
Bearer path executed_by was subject-only. Add an identity enricher that calls the
IdP userinfo endpoint with the caller's access token to fetch the profile, mirroring
how cloud resolves a subject to a full user (cloud uses its identity service; the
standalone runs service queries the IdP directly).

- identity_enricher.go: resolves userinfo_endpoint from OIDC discovery (cached),
  GETs userinfo with the forwarded access token, caches subject->identity (10m TTL),
  and is fully best-effort — any timeout/error/missing-claim falls back to the
  subject-only identity and never blocks run creation. Driven by the existing
  runs.authMetadata.externalAuthServerBaseUrl; nil (no-op) when unset.
- CreateRun enriches the parsed identity using the Bearer token or the ALB-forwarded
  X-Amzn-Oidc-Accesstoken. The cookie path already carries claims via x-amzn-oidc-data,
  so it short-circuits (hasProfile) without an extra call.
- Removed the temporary AUTHDEBUG diagnostic.

Mount the whole co-pilot Secret instead of a pinned key

copilotStorageSecretRef names a Secret that exists to hold co-pilot's storage
configuration, so its keys are co-pilot's to name. Pinning the projection to
copilot-storage-config.yaml made a Secret whose key was named anything else
fail to mount, and ruled out splitting the config across several ordered keys
even though flytestdlib globs MountPath/*.yaml and merges one viper per file.

Project the whole Secret and let the glob decide what is read. Verified on a
cluster: both .yaml keys are matched in sorted order and a non-.yaml key is
mounted but ignored. The chart still writes a single copilot-storage-config
.yaml key, which is now a chart-local choice rather than a plugin contract.

flyte-binary-v2: save CPU base to Depot ephemeral registry

buildx refuses local OCI export for multi-node multi-arch builds
(error: "oci for multi-node builds currently not supported"), and
Depot intentionally uses one native node per platform. Switch the
CPU build to Depot's ephemeral registry via `save: true` and a
unique per-run tag, and have the GPU build resolve `FROM` directly
from `registry.depot.dev/<project>:<tag>` — auth is implicit since
both builds run in the same Depot project. Drops the OCI tarball
extract step and the build-contexts indirection.

Refs: https://github.com/docker/buildx/discussions/2351

fix(spark): apply platform scheduling after custom driver/executor pod merge

createDriverSpec/createExecutorSpec merge the custom driver/executor k8s_pod onto
the base pod (MergeOverlayPodSpecOntoBase) but re-applied no scheduling afterward,
unlike Ray. A driver/executor whose custom pod carries its own node-affinity term
therefore lost the default-affinity and (non)interruptible requirements via the
same OR-append dilution, e.g. an executor under interruptible=false could still be
scheduled on a spot node.

Call flytek8s.ApplyPlatformSchedulingConstraints after each merge (driver forced
non-interruptible, executor following the task flag). Idempotent, so the no-custom-
pod path is unchanged.

Adds TestBuildResourceSparkExecutorAffinityDilution reproducing the executor
dilution.

feat: LogContext.pod_name_prefix is repeated

A single prefix cannot describe tasks whose pods live under more than one
name — e.g. a job submitted to a shared, autoscaling cluster has its own
submitter pod plus cluster pods that may not exist yet (so enumerating
them is insufficient). The first element is the task's own pod-name
prefix; plugins may append auxiliary prefixes. This also removes the need
for per-plugin prefix stamping — reverted here — since the framework can
own the primary element.

Fix actor slow startup times (#621)

## Overview
Somewhere along the way a regression on actor performance occurred (probably during my large refactor). Cold-start times are extremely large as a result of reporting 0 capacity for the initial heartbeat. This means we need to wait for the next heartbeat for an updated capacity report to assign any tasks to the worker.

The problem is that the executor startup was in a race condition with the heartbeat mechanism, so if the rust worker heartbeat before executors were initialized then the capacity was 0. This PR adds a future over a boolean to determine whether the runtime has initialized before starting the heartbeat runtime.

## Test Plan
Ran this locally and decreased cold-start for "hello world" from 16s to 2s. Going to run some tests on cloud to make sure.

fix(executor): wait out RetryStrategy.backoff between user retries (#8097)

* fix(executor): wait out RetryStrategy.backoff between user retries

#7308 added `RetryStrategy.backoff` to the protos and the SDKs serialize
it, but the executor relaunched a failed attempt on its next reconcile
regardless, so retries fired back-to-back at the requeue interval.

Stamp `Status.NextAttemptAt` when a user retry is scheduled, from both
the in-place restart and the max-runtime timeout paths, using
`min(base * factor**n, cap)` for the n-th retry as the SDKs document.
While it lies in the future the reconcile requeues for the remainder
instead of handling the plugin; it is cleared when the attempt launches.
Tasks without a backoff are unchanged.

Signed-off-by: Chris Thomas <chris.john.thomas@gmail.com>

* fix(executor): reject a retry backoff the proto contract rejects

Validate TaskMetadata.retries.backoff in validateTaskAction against the
rules on Backoff in flyteidl2/core/literals.proto: non-negative base and
cap, a finite factor >= 1, and a cap whenever factor > 1. A bad template
now fails the TaskAction as InvalidSpec, like an invalid timeout, instead
of growing the delay unbounded and clamping it at the maximum duration.

Signed-off-by: Chris Thomas <chris.john.thomas@gmail.com>

* fix(executor): gate the retry backoff before building plugin state

The backoff check needs neither the PluginStateManager nor the
TaskExecutionContext, so run it straight after the finalizer check.
NextAttemptAt and TimeoutAt are never both set, as both retry paths
clear TimeoutAt when they stamp NextAttemptAt, so its order against the
timeout-cleanup resume does not matter.

Signed-off-by: Chris Thomas <chris.john.thomas@gmail.com>

* fix(executor): requeue a timed-out retry when its backoff ends

An immediate requeue after a timed-out attempt is retried only reached
the backoff gate and requeued again. Wait out the backoff directly,
keeping the immediate requeue for retries without one.

Signed-off-by: Chris Thomas <chris.john.thomas@gmail.com>

* test(executor): cover the retry backoff after a max-runtime timeout

The existing spec drives the in-place restart path only. Walk a
timed-out attempt through its retry: the timeout reconcile schedules the
retry 10s out and requeues for it, an early reconcile waits the
remainder without handling the plugin, and the retry launches on time.

Render copilot Secret in the task namespace, trim the diff

The co-pilot storage Secret was rendered into .Release.Namespace while task
pods are created in flyte-core-components.actions.kubernetes.namespace, which
defaults to the literal "flyte". A pod can only project Secrets from its own
namespace, so any install outside "flyte" left every co-pilot task pod stuck
in ContainerCreating on FailedMount. Render it where the pods are, and note on
the values key that a non-release namespace must exist before helm install.

Extract the stow storage block into a shared named template, parameterised by
whether to inline the S3 credentials, so the ConfigMap and the Secret cannot
drift. Renders byte-identically across s3+accesskey, s3+iam, gcs, azure and
the copilotStorageSecretRef path; the bundled devbox manifest is regenerated
for the comment change alone.

Drop the unused ctx from FlyteCoPilotContainer and CopilotCommandArgs. It was
plumbed in for a warning that was never written, and removing it restores
FlyteCoPilotContainer to its original signature. Inline the single-use
keyToPaths helper and the unreachable empty-secret branch in
storageConfigVolume, and cut the comments back to the constraints the code
cannot show on its own.

`created_at < cursor`, so any rows sharing the boundary row's created_at were
skipped across pages. Map-task children are created in bulk with (nearly)
identical created_at, so a run's ListActions/ListRuns could under-report.

Encode the full default sort key (phase, created_at, run_name, name) in an
opaque cursor token and expand the keyset by hand (Postgres row-value
comparison can't mix ASC/DESC). (run_name, name) is unique per row (part of
the PK), giving a total order so tied created_at never skips a page boundary.
The default ORDER BY gains (run_name DESC, name DESC) tiebreakers to match, and
a cursor with a custom sort is now rejected since the keyset assumes the
default order.

Executor webhook: pluggable pod/node mutators and v1 secret-injection fixes (#8137)

Webhook: serve extra mutators and port v1 secret-injection fixes

The executor's pod webhook only ever served the secrets mutator. Deployments
that embed it (Union's single-binary onebox, and eventually its data plane in
place of the flytepropeller v1 webhook) need to add their own pod and node
mutators, and need the fixes the v1 webhook accumulated.

Handlers:
- PodMutator / NodeMutator interfaces and a generic handler; each mutator is
  its own MutatingWebhook with its own path (/mutate--v1-<kind>/<id>), name
  and object selector.
- Setup/NewWebhook take options: WithPodMutators, WithNodeMutators,
  WithHandlers (custom name/paths), WithLimitNamespace.
- The secrets handler keeps /mutate--v1-pod and is also served at
  /mutate--v1-pod/secrets, the path charts that render the configuration
  themselves use. webhookTimeout is applied to every webhook.

Secrets (ported from the v1 webhook):
- clusterName and the cluster-scoped eager API key lookup.
- The image-pull Secret informer is only started when needed and is scoped
  to the limit namespace.
- InitCerts keeps a valid existing cert Secret instead of regenerating on
  every start (which churned the CA bundle under running replicas).

fix(helm): add cloudwatch region and logGroup fields to flyte-binary chart

The flyte-binary chart only supported cloudwatch-template-uri for
CloudWatch log configuration, requiring users to embed the region and
log group directly in a URL template string. When users deployed the
eks example files without replacing the <AWS_REGION> and
<EKS_CLUSTER_NAME> placeholders, these literal strings appeared
URL-encoded in the Flyte UI CloudWatch links.

Add dedicated cloudwatch.region and cloudwatch.logGroup fields to the
chart, mirroring the configuration surface already available in
flyte-core. When these fields are set, the chart emits
cloudwatch-region and cloudwatch-log-group config keys. The existing
templateUri field is preserved for full backward compatibility and
takes precedence when set.

Update eks-production.yaml and eks-starter.yaml to use the new fields.

fix: honour the declared primary container of a custom spark pod spec

A custom driver/executor pod spec carries the container the user calls
primary, in core.K8SPod.primary_container_name, and the plugin read it
nowhere. Spark was left to guess with its first-container default even
though the answer was on the object.

Pass it through as spark.kubernetes.{driver,executor}
.podTemplateContainerName. A name that is absent from the spec costs
nothing: Spark warns and falls back to the first container, which is what
happened before. An unset name still leaves the conf unset.

headless name to every pod, the ClusterIP entry is unreachable dead config --
and a trap: pointing webhookURL at the ClusterIP Service would load-balance to
one replica and silently leave the rest serving stale secrets.

invalidation. The container still declares containerPort 9444.

docs: add FLYTE_IMAGE_REGISTRY setup step for remote workflow execution

When running workflows remotely on a demo cluster using ImageSpec,
pyflyte needs FLYTE_IMAGE_REGISTRY set to push the container image to
the local registry. Without this, tasks that reference
os.environ['FLYTE_IMAGE_REGISTRY'] fail at runtime.

Add a step to export FLYTE_IMAGE_REGISTRY=localhost:30000 before
pyflyte run, and pass it via --env so task containers also have
access to the variable. Fix the pre-existing step numbering error
(steps jumped from 4 back to 3).

Closes #6606

correct when the query is ordered by exactly (created_at ASC, name ASC). ListActions
is a shared method, so a future caller passing KeysetAfter with a different sort would
silently skip/duplicate rows. Reject that combination instead of trusting the caller.

storage: bump stow to v0.5.1 to stream S3 uploads of files instead of buffering them

stow v0.5.1 (flyteorg/stow#32): since v0.5.0, the S3 provider read each
body below 16 MiB fully into memory and allocated 48 MiB of part buffers up
front for larger ones, even for an *os.File. Seekable bodies are now
uploaded straight from the file: one PutObject below the threshold, and a
multipart upload of section readers above it.

This bounds the copilot uploader's memory per file regardless of file size,
complementing the concurrency cap from #8149.

fix(devbox): stage the kubeconfig where the caller can write it

devbox-functional-tests failed on `make devbox-run`:

    Waiting for kubeconfig...
    /bin/sh: 1: cannot create /home/runner/work/flyte/flyte/.kube/kubeconfig: Permission denied

Docker creates the bind-mount source directory as root when it starts the
container. The previous code never wrote there from the host — the container
wrote the file as root and `start` chowned it — so reading the kubeconfig out of
the container and redirecting into that directory only worked where the dir
already existed owned by the caller, which is true locally and false on a fresh
runner.

Stage it under $(HOME)/.kube instead, which the caller owns by definition, and
merge from there. The chown of the bind-mounted copy comes back so that
`make kubeconfig` still has a readable file (k3s writes it 0600 root), but is
now tolerated to fail, since that path does not exist when the devbox mounts a
different dir — the case the original fix was for.

Reproduced the CI condition locally by making the directory unwritable
(chmod 500): the old path fails to create the file, `make devbox-run` now
completes, the devbox is reachable, and ~/.kube/config keeps all 8 contexts.

fix(copilot): stage set Optional[File] inputs like File under NAMED_DIR

Under the NAMED_DIR layout a single File input is staged inside a
per-input directory under its original basename (/var/inputs/<var>/<name>),
which is what shell tasks glob for (/var/inputs/<var>/*). singleBlob only
recognised a bare blob literal, though, and an Optional[File] input is
serialized as a union wrapping the blob. So a set optional file fell
through to the plain path and was written as /var/inputs/<var> itself: the
glob matched nothing and the script silently behaved as if the input were
unset (e.g. STAR dropped mate 2 of a paired-end sample; salmon index
skipped its decoy genome).

Unwrap union literals in singleBlob so a set Optional[File] stages exactly
like a File. An unset optional (union of none) is unchanged and never
becomes a per-input directory.

under the wrong section and had to carry a copilot prefix to say so. Under the
co-pilot section it is just storageSecretRef, the same way the Go field became
StorageConfigSecretName once it lived in FlyteCoPilotConfig.

repeating the index dance at four call sites.

Renders are byte-identical for every valid combination, and the gate matrix
is unchanged: a supplied ref still suppresses the chart's own Secret, and the
install still fails when combined with external configuration.

fix(executor): measure GPU fault relevance from the failure, not from now

The relevance window compared a fault's last observation against the
classification time, which answers "was this fault recent when we looked"
rather than "did this fault precede this failure closely enough". A slow
reconcile could age a real cause out, and a fault observed after the
failure could be credited to it. The window is now measured from the
failure's own time, taken from the pod plugin's TaskInfo.OccurredAt (the
container termination the kubelet stamped on the same node as the fault
events), with a short slack for a fault recorded moments after the
failure it caused and nothing beyond that; a future-dated event can no
longer stay relevant indefinitely. The classification time is only the
fallback when a plugin stamped no occurrence time.

The identity comments are tightened to match the code: an event without a
regarding UID is rejected outright, and the name-only match when the pod's
own UID is unknown is stated as the deliberate trade it is.
